title: Balanceboard: Latency vs Cost Aperture Scan (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This is a quick exploratory brief (working draft) on a 'balanceboard' style aperture scan: how latency percentiles and marginal per-token cost trade across three knobs simultaneously — batch size, kv-cache hit rate, and prefetch window. Audience: Console, Optimize, and serving-runtime owners who want a lightweight artifact to show in triage/roadmap sync.

TL;DR (one paragraph):
We see a clear bifurcation: for low-latency tiers (p50 < 30ms) marginal cost increases rapidly with batch size and aggressive prefetching, while for cost-first tiers the same knobs deliver 18–26% token-cost savings at p95 degradation limited to ~12–18% depending on cache hit. Medium cache-hit (60–80%) is the most forgiving region — 8–12% cost saved with p95 impact under 10% for moderate batching.

Experiment setup (short):
- Date range: sampled windowed runs on 2029-07-09 through 2029-07-11.
- Infra: Dedicated G5x2 pools (default kernel set), controlled same model variant (open-llama-40b-quant8), synthetic client generator to simulate sessionized chat patterns (60/30/10 short/med/long turns).
- Knobs swept: batch_size = [1,4,8,16], kv_cache_hit = [20, 50, 80, 95] percent, prefetch_window = [0, 4, 12] tokens.
- Measured: p50/p90/p95 latency (ms), tokens-per-dollar (inverted cost), per-request tail penalty (% increase relative to baseline batch=1, cache=95).
- Notes: no concurrency limiting aside from client; cold start excluded. All runs warm.

Workload profile (text table):
TurnType | Fraction | AvgPromptLen | AvgGenLen
short    | 0.60     | 20           | 16
med      | 0.30     | 64           | 48
long     | 0.10     | 240          | 160

Representative numeric excerpt (median across repeated runs):
Batch | Cache% | Prefetch | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tokens/$ (relative)
1     | 95     | 0        | 18      | 38      | 1.00
4     | 80     | 4        | 26      | 56      | 1.12
8     | 60     | 12       | 38      | 82      | 1.22
16    | 50     | 12       | 62      | 140     | 1.30

Key qualitative observations:
- p50 rises smoothly with batch size; p95 is non-linear and often dominated by queueing spikes when cache-hit < 70%.
- Prefetch helps tokens/$ more at higher cache hits, but it amplifies p95 when batch > 8. That suggests interaction between prefetch kernel path and batching serialization.
- For strict low-latency tiers (target p95 < 60ms), useful operating region is: batch <= 4 and cache hit >= 80%. Here we get modest cost savings (~8–12%) with acceptable percentile impact.
- For cost-first tier (no hard p95), batch=8 + prefetch=12 + cache>=60% yields the best token/$ improvement in these experiments (~20–26%).

ASCII heatmap (p95 latency impact vs batch and cache). Legend: . = <50ms, o = 50–80ms, O = 80–120ms, X = >120ms
Cache% \ Batch | 1  4  8   16
95%           | .  .  o   O
80%           | .  o  O   X
60%           | o  O  X   X
20%           | O  X  X   X

Mini-sparkline (tokens/$ relative) across batch sizes for cache=80%, prefetch=4:
batch=1: ▁▁▂▃ (1.00)
batch=4: ▂▃▅▆ (1.12)
batch=8: ▅▆▆█ (1.18)

Tradeoff matrix (short bullets):
- Priority: LowLatency -> knobs: batch=1..4, prefetch=0..4, invest in cache hit (policy)
- Priority: LowCost -> knobs: batch=8..16, prefetch=8..12, accept p95 uplift and add tiered fallback
- Priority: Robustness -> knobs: batch small, prefetch small, multi-variant routing (fallback to unquantized)

Interpretation / root causes (hypotheses):
- Kernel fusion for prefetch path performs best when kv cache lookup cost is amortized across tokens — high cache-hit is required. When cache misses are common, prefetch work becomes wasted and increases memory traffic, leading to long tail.
- Batching beyond a threshold (observed ~8 for this HW) increases scheduling jitter under bursty sessionized traffic. The runtime's admission path currently doesn't smooth these microbursts, producing long p95 tails.

Actionable next steps (short list):
1) Console: provide a quick 'balanceboard' toggle in the SLO builder: preset(LowLatency), preset(LowCost), and a slider to visualize expected p95 uplift for target token/$ curves. (owner: Console PM)
2) Serving-runtime: instrument batch admission histogram and add a small jittering backoff to avoid synchronized enqueue spikes (owner: serving-runtime).
3) Optimize: run targeted kernel profiling for prefetch path on cache/hit <-> miss transitions; identify memory-copy hotspots. (owner: Optimize/Applied-ML)
4) Product: add a recommended config doc for Dedicated customers with sessionized chat patterns (owner: Product - Hosted API/Dedicated).

Open questions / things to validate:
- Repeat this sweep with a different quantized variant and a different hardware class (A100 vs G5) — kernels may show different breakpoints.
- How does client-level multiplexing (multiple logical sessions per connection) change the observed tail shapes?

Appendix: quick run links (lab notes):
- raw CSVs: s3://redwood-perf/2029-07/balanceboard-run-*/metrics.csv
- summary notebook: https://notebooks.redwood.internal/balanceboard-2029-07
- next PR (perf infra): GITHUB:repo/perf/PR#421

Notes to self: still want a small violin PNG for deck; ASCII heatmap is OK for quick sync but won't make marketing collateral. Keep this doc as the canonical experimental log until we finalize a condensed one-pager for customers.
